- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified.   assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."

- <example>

  <commentary>

This includes checking for common security vulnerabilities, validating input handling, reviewing authentication/authorization implementations, scanning for hardcoded secrets, and ensuring OWASP compliance. <example>Context: The user wants to ensure their newly implemented API endpoints are secure before deployment.
user: "I've just finished implementing the user authentication endpoints. Can you check them for security issues?"
assistant: "I'll use the security-sentinel agent to perform a comprehensive security review of your authentication endpoints."
<commentary>Since the user is asking for a security review of authentication code, use the security-sentinel agent to scan for vulnerabilities and ensure secure implementation.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is concerned about potential SQL injection vulnerabilities in their database queries.
user: "I'm worried about SQL injection in our search functionality. Can you review it?"
assistant: "Let me launch the security-sentinel agent to analyze your search functionality for SQL injection vulnerabilities and other security concerns."
<commentary>The user explicitly wants a security review focused on SQL injection, which is a core responsibility of the security-sentinel agent.</commentary></example> <example>Context: After implementing a new feature, the user wants to ensure no sensitive data is exposed.
user: "I've added the payment processing module. Please check if any sensitive data might be exposed."
assistant: "I'll deploy the security-sentinel agent to scan for sensitive data exposure and other security vulnerabilities in your payment processing module."
<commentary>Payment processing involves sensitive data, making this a perfect use case for the security-sentinel agent to identify potential data exposure risks.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:bug-reproduction-validator: Use this agent when you receive a bug report or issue description and need to verify whether the reported behavior is actually a bug. This agent will attempt to reproduce the issue systematically, validate the steps to reproduce, and confirm whether the behavior deviates from expected functionality. <example>
Context: The user has reported a potential bug in the application.
user: "Users are reporting that the email processing fails when there are special characters in the subject line"
assistant: "I'll use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to verify if this is an actual bug by attempting to reproduce it"
<commentary>
Since there's a bug report about email processing with special characters, use the bug-reproduction-validator agent to systematically reproduce and validate the issue.
</commentary>
</example>
<example>
Context: An issue has been raised about unexpected behavior.
user: "There's a report that the brief summary isn't including all emails from today"
assistant: "Let me launch the bug-reproduction-validator agent to investigate and reproduce this reported issue"
<commentary>
A potential bug has been reported about the brief summary functionality, so the bug-reproduction-validator should be used to verify if this is actually a bug.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:every-style-editor: Use this agent when you need to review and edit text content to conform to Every's specific style guide. This includes reviewing articles, blog posts, newsletters, documentation, or any written content that needs to follow Every's editorial standards. The agent will systematically check for title case in headlines, sentence case elsewhere, company singular/plural usage, overused words, passive voice, number formatting, punctuation rules, and other style guide requirements. (Tools: Task, Glob, Grep, LS, ExitPlanMode, Read, Edit, MultiEdit, Write, NotebookRead, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch)
- entire-engineering:workflow:lint: Use this agent when you need to run linting and code quality checks on Ruby and ERB files. Run before pushing to origin. (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:pr-comment-resolver: Use this agent when you need to address comments on pull requests or code reviews by making the requested changes and reporting back on the resolution. This agent handles the full workflow of understanding the comment, implementing the fix, and providing a clear summary of what was done. <example>Context: A reviewer has left a comment on a pull request asking for a specific change to be made.user: "The reviewer commented that we should add error handling to the payment processing method"assistant: "I'll use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address this comment by implementing the error handling and reporting back"<commentary>Since there's a PR comment that needs to be addressed with code changes, use the pr-comment-resolver agent to handle the implementation and resolution.</commentary></example><example>Context: Multiple code review comments need to be addressed systematically.user: "Can you fix the issues mentioned in the code review? They want better variable names and to extract the validation logic"assistant: "Let me use the pr-comment-resolver agent to address these review comments one by one"<commentary>The user wants to resolve code review feedback, so the pr-comment-resolver agent should handle making the changes and reporting on each resolution.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:workflow:spec-flow-analyzer: Use this agent when you have a specification, plan, feature description, or technical document that needs user flow analysis and gap identification. This agent should be used proactively when:

<example>
Context: The user has just finished drafting a specification for OAuth implementation.
user: "Here's the OAuth spec for our new integration:
[OAuth spec details]"
assistant: "Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze this OAuth specification for user flows and missing elements."
<commentary>
Since the user has provided a specification document, use the Task tool to launch the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and missing clarifications.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user is planning a new social sharing feature.
user: "I'm thinking we should add social sharing to posts. Users can share to Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn."
assistant: "This sounds like a feature specification that would benefit from flow analysis. Let me use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to map out all the user flows and identify any missing pieces."
<commentary>
The user is describing a new feature. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to analyze the feature from the user's perspective, identify all permutations, and surface questions about missing elements.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: The user has created a plan for a new onboarding flow.
user: "Can you review this onboarding plan and make sure we haven't missed anything?"
assistant: "I'll use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to thoroughly analyze this onboarding plan from the user's perspective."
<commentary>
The user is explicitly asking for review of a plan. Use the spec-flow-analyzer agent to identify all user flows, edge cases, and gaps in the specification.
</commentary>
</example>

Call this agent when:
- A user presents a feature specification, plan, or requirements document
- A user asks to review or validate a design or implementation plan
- A user describes a new feature or integration that needs flow analysis
- After initial planning sessions to validate completeness
- Before implementation begins on complex user-facing features
- When stakeholders need clarity on user journeys and edge cases (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- posthog:error-analyzer: Analyze multiple PostHog errors in parallel to identify patterns, root causes, and prioritize fixes based on user impact. (Tools: All tools)
- reviewer: Code review agent - critically reviews changes for quality, security, and correctness (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- test-doc: Use this agent when the user needs markdown files created in the test-files/ directory. This includes generating test data files, sample documentation, mock content, or any markdown-formatted files for testing purposes.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User needs sample markdown files for testing a documentation parser.
user: "I need some sample markdown files to test my parser"
assistant: "I'll use the markdown-file-generator agent to create sample markdown files in the test-files/ directory for your parser testing."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

Context: User is setting up test fixtures and needs markdown content.
user: "Create a few test markdown files with different heading levels and formatting"
assistant: "Let me use the markdown-file-generator agent to create markdown files with varied formatting in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User needs mock README files for testing.
user: "Generate some fake README files for my test suite"
assistant: "I'll invoke the markdown-file-generator agent to create mock README files in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

## plugin:entire-engineering:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- diagnose: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Reproduce → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. Use when user says "diagnose this" / "debug this", reports a bug, says something is broken/throwing/failing, or describes a performance regression.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- github-triage: Triage GitHub issues through a label-based state machine. Use when user wants to create an issue, triage issues, review incoming bugs or feature requests, prepare issues for an AFK agent, or manage issue workflow.
- review-pr-feedback: Walk every unresolved review thread on the current branch's PR — fix what is fixable, ask the user about anything ambiguous, then reply on each thread and mark it resolved. Use when the user says "review PR feedback", "go thru the PR comments", "address review comments", or similar.
- ship: Commit, push, and update the PR description or add a comment based on new changes. Use when the user says "ship it", "commit push and update pr", or similar.
- to-issues: Break a plan, spec, or PRD into independently-grabbable GitHub issues using tracer-bullet vertical slices. Use when user wants to convert a plan into issues, create implementation tickets, or break down work into issues.
- to-prd: Turn the current conversation context into a PRD and submit it as a GitHub issue. Use when user wants to create a PRD from the current context.
- unslop: Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.
- write-a-skill: Create new agent skills with proper structure, progressive disclosure, and bundled resources. Use when user wants to create, write, or build a new skill.
- agent-integration: Run all three agent integration phases sequentially: research, write-tests, and implement using E2E-first TDD (unit tests written last). For individual phases, use /agent-integration:research, /agent-integration:write-tests, or /agent-integration:implement. Use when the user says "integrate agent", "add agent support", or wants to run the full agent integration pipeline end-to-end.
- changelog: Generate or update the CHANGELOG.md for a new release version. Use when the user says "generate changelog", "update changelog", "write release notes", or asks to prepare a changelog for a version like "changelog for 0.5.3".
- e2e: Orchestrate E2E test triage and fix implementation: runs triage-ci then implement sequentially. Accepts test names, --agent, artifact path, or CI run reference. For individual phases, use /e2e:triage-ci, /e2e:debug, or /e2e:implement. Use when the user says "triage e2e", "fix e2e failures", or wants the full triage-to-fix pipeline.
- test-repo: Use this skill to test strategy changes against a fresh test repository. Invoke when the user asks to "test against a test repo", "validate the changes", or wants to verify session hooks, commits, and rewind functionality work correctly.

+package opencode
+
+import (
+	"fmt"
+	"os"
+	"path/filepath"
+	"time"
+)
+
+// exportStagePrefix marks a transient, half-written export under .entire/tmp.
+//
+// The leading "." and the absence of a ".json" suffix are load-bearing: everything
+// else in .entire/tmp is created-and-left, and the directory is scanned by name by
+// FindActivePreTaskFile (pre-task-*.json) and by `entire clean --all`. A staged
+// export must not look like either.
+const exportStagePrefix = ".export-"
+
+// renameRetries bounds how long we wait out a Windows sharing violation. On POSIX
+// the first attempt either succeeds or fails for a reason retrying cannot fix.
+const (
+	renameRetries = 5
+	renameBackoff = 40 * time.Millisecond
+)
+
+// stageExportPath creates an empty staging file in dir for sessionID's export and
+// returns its path. The caller must remove it unless it installs it.
+func stageExportPath(dir, sessionID string) (string, error) {
+	file, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, exportStagePrefix+sessionID+"-*")
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("failed to create export staging file: %w", err)
+	}
+	if err := file.Close(); err != nil {
+		_ = os.Remove(file.Name())
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("failed to create export staging file: %w", err)
+	}
+	return file.Name(), nil
+}
+
+// renameOverExisting moves staged onto dest, replacing it, and fsyncs dest's
+// directory so the replacement survives a crash.
+//
+// On Windows the replace can lose a race that does not exist on POSIX: os.Rename
+// there is MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING), which must delete dest, and Go
+// opens files without FILE_SHARE_DELETE — so any concurrent reader of dest (an
+// `entire attach` in another terminal, the condensation path reading the same
+// transcript) makes the rename fail with a sharing violation where the older
+// in-place write would have succeeded. Readers of a transcript hold it briefly, so
+// a bounded retry covers the realistic case; a reader that holds it longer gets a
+// clear error and a preserved staging file rather than a lost transcript.
+func renameOverExisting(staged, dest string) error {
+	var err error
+	for range renameRetries {
+		if err = os.Rename(staged, dest); err == nil {
+			syncDir(filepath.Dir(dest))
+			return nil
+		}
+		if !isRenameContention(err) {
+			return fmt.Errorf("failed to install export file: %w", err)
+		}
+		time.Sleep(renameBackoff)
+	}
+	return fmt.Errorf("%w (another process may be reading %s)", err, filepath.Base(dest))
+}
+
+// syncDir flushes a directory entry so a completed rename is not lost by a crash.
+// Best-effort: directory fsync is not supported everywhere (notably Windows), and
+// failing to durably record an export is not worth failing the export over.
+func syncDir(dir string) {
+	// Same shape as the directory fsync in jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic.
+	if d, err := os.Open(dir); err == nil { //nolint:gosec // G304: dir is the .entire/tmp path the caller just wrote into, not user input
+		_ = d.Sync() //nolint:errcheck // best-effort directory fsync; failure does not roll back the rename
+		_ = d.Close()
+	}
+}

+package opencode

+import (

+	"syscall"
+)
+
+// Windows error codes MoveFileEx returns when it cannot delete the destination
+// because another handle is open on it. ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED is included because
+// MoveFileEx reports it for a destination opened without FILE_SHARE_DELETE.
+const (
+	errorAccessDenied     syscall.Errno = 5
+	errorSharingViolation syscall.Errno = 32
+)
+
+// isRenameContention reports whether err is a transient sharing failure worth
+// retrying. See renameOverExisting for why this only ever fires on Windows.
+func isRenameContention(err error) bool {
+	var errno syscall.Errno
+	if !errors.As(err, &errno) {
+		return false
+	}
+	return errno == errorSharingViolation || errno == errorAccessDenied
+}

+// transcript) makes the rename fail with a sharing violation where the older
+// in-place write would have succeeded. Readers of a transcript hold it briefly, so
+// a bounded retry covers the realistic case; a reader that holds it longer gets a
+// clear error and a preserved staging file rather than a lost transcript.
+func renameOverExisting(staged, dest string) error {
+	var err error
+	for range renameRetries {
+		if err = os.Rename(staged, dest); err == nil {
+			syncDir(filepath.Dir(dest))
+			return nil
+		}
+		if !isRenameContention(err) {
+			return fmt.Errorf("failed to install export file: %w", err)
+		}
+		time.Sleep(renameBackoff)
+	}
+	return fmt.Errorf("%w (another process may be reading %s)", err, filepath.Base(dest))
+}
+
+// syncDir flushes a directory entry so a completed rename is not lost by a crash.
+// Best-effort: directory fsync is not supported everywhere (notably Windows), and
+// failing to durably record an export is not worth failing the export over.
+func syncDir(dir string) {
+	// Same shape as the directory fsync in jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic.
+	if d, err := os.Open(dir); err == nil { //nolint:gosec // G304: dir is the .entire/tmp path the caller just wrote into, not user input
+		_ = d.Sync() //nolint:errcheck // best-effort directory fsync; failure does not roll back the rename
+		_ = d.Close()
+	}
+}

**What it enables:** A pre-read synchronization step before the framework reads the transcript.

**What it enables:** Includes files modified by spawned subagents in the checkpoint file list and aggregates subagent token usage.

Reviewed all 5 commits (13 files, +1038/−50). Verified: `go build ./...`, `GOOS=windows go build ./...`, `go test` on `agent/`, `agent/opencode/`, and the attach/clean tests, plus `golangci-lint 2.11.3 run ./cmd/entire/cli/...` → 0 issues.

## Verdict

The core of this is right, and the sequencing across the five commits is the good kind of paranoid. Three things stand out as genuinely well-judged:

- **Staging before install** (`stage_export.go` + `fetchAndCacheExport`). The old code wrote `opencode export` straight over `.entire/tmp/<session>.json` and `os.Remove`d it on failure — so a missing binary or a 30s timeout destroyed what is often the only local copy of the session. Validating JSON on the staging path and only then renaming closes both the truncated-payload and zero-exit-empty holes, and `keepStaged = true` on rename failure (with the path in the error) is the correct call over deleting a validated export.
- **`lookupLocalOnly` vs `lookupAllowFetch`.** Gating fetch on "the agent the user actually named" is what keeps `detectAgentByTranscript` from spawning a 30s subprocess and creating `.entire/tmp` for every registered agent on a typo'd session ID. `TestResolveAndValidateTranscript_LocalOnlyDoesNotFetch` pins it.
- **`TranscriptFetcher` as a builtin-only capability** (no `DeclaredCaps` gate) matches the existing precedent for `TranscriptSanitizer`/`ModelExtractor`, and the comment in `capabilities.go` was updated rather than left stale.

The Windows `isRenameContention` split is correctly reasoned — `MoveFileEx(REPLACE_EXISTING)` really does have to delete the destination, and Go really does omit `FILE_SHARE_DELETE` — and POSIX correctly returns `false` so no retry loop runs where it can't help.

## Findings

**1. Undocumented optional interface — `docs/architecture/agent-guide.md`**
Every other optional interface has a row in the "Optional Interfaces" table (line ~46) and a dedicated section (`TranscriptPreparer` at line 475). `TranscriptFetcher` has neither, and `agent-integration-checklist.md:44` still points only at `TranscriptAnalyzer`/`TranscriptPreparer`. This is the repo's own convention for a new agent capability, and the distinction from `TranscriptPreparer` ("refreshes an existing file" vs "conjures one that never existed") is exactly what a future integrator needs written down.

**2. Doubled error prefix — `stage_export.go:60` + `lifecycle.go:270`**
`renameOverExisting` returns `fmt.Errorf("failed to install export file: %w", err)`, and the caller wraps it again with the same words:

```
failed to install export file (export saved at .../.export-ses_x-123): failed to install export file: permission denied
```

Drop the prefix from one of the two — the caller's version is the one carrying the recovery path, so `renameOverExisting` should just return the bare wrapped error.

**3. `unprobedFetcherHint` fires on every miss, including plain typos — `attach.go:793`**
`entire attach <typo>` under the default agent now always ends with `opencode can export transcripts on demand — retry with --agent opencode`. For the case it was written for (right session, wrong agent) it's a good hint; for a mistyped Claude Code UUID it sends the user down a wrong path. Worth considering gating on something cheap — e.g. only when the session ID doesn't match the named agent's ID shape — but this is a product judgment call, not a defect, so flagging rather than deciding.

**4. Ctrl-C during export produces a compound message — `attach.go:889`**
The `context.Canceled` early return is *not* wrapped in `transcriptFetchError`, so it misses the suppression branch at line 772. `detectAgentByTranscript` then runs on a dead context (it only stats files, so it never notices) and its failure gets appended:

```
fetch transcript: context canceled (also tried auto-detecting other agents: transcript not found for any registered agent)
```

Cosmetic, but it's the one path where the new suppression logic doesn't do what its comment says.

Nothing here is a correctness bug in the staging or install path — the four regression tests (`PartialFailure`, `TruncatedZeroExit`, `EmptyZeroExit`, `InstallsValidExport`) each assert on the cached transcript's contents afterward, which is the assertion that actually matters, and the `InstallsValidExport` stub checking mid-flight that the live file is untouched is a nice touch. The `clean.go` `IsNotExist` tolerance is the right narrow fix for the race the staging introduces.

content.content:
- Parse the native format when CLI features need specific data (e.g., extract file paths for `entire status`)
- Let the backend normalize formats for display

**Don't:**
- Create a "universal transcript format" in the CLI
- Transform logs to match what the web UI expects
- Strip or restructure data to simplify backend processing
- Create intermediate formats (e.g., converting JSON to JSONL for "easier parsing")
- Reconstruct transcripts from events when a canonical export exists

## Integration Checklist

### Transcript Capture

See Guide: [Transcript Format Guide](agent-guide.md#transcript-format-guide), [TranscriptAnalyzer](agent-guide.md#transcriptanalyzer), [TranscriptPreparer](agent-guide.md#transcriptpreparer)

- [ ] **Full transcript on every turn**: At turn-end, capture the complete session transcript, not just events since the last checkpoint
- [ ] **Resumed session handling**: When a user resumes an existing session, the transcript must include all historical messages, not just new ones since the plugin/hook loaded
- [ ] **Use agent's canonical export**: Prefer the agent's native export command (e.g., reading Claude's JSONL file, Gemini's JSON, Cursor's JSONL, Factory AI Droid's JSONL, Copilot CLI's JSONL, OpenCode's `opencode export` JSON, Pi's JSONL session file) over manually reconstructing from events
- [ ] **No custom formats**: Store the agent's native format directly in `NativeData` - do not convert between formats (e.g., JSON to JSONL) or create intermediate representations
- [ ] **Graceful degradation**: If the canonical source is unavailable (e.g., agent shutting down), fall back to best-effort capture with clear documentation of limitations

### Session Storage Abstraction

See Guide: [Step 3 - Core Agent Interface](agent-guide.md#step-3-implement-core-agent-interface-youragentgo)

input.description: Read commit message for auto-detection fix

content.content:
fix(attach): keep auto-detection from exporting on the user's behalf

detectAgentByTranscript probes every registered agent through
resolveAndValidateTranscript, so making OpenCode a TranscriptFetcher meant any
failed attach — of any agent — ran `opencode export <that-session-id>` as a side
effect of detection: a subprocess with a 30s timeout ceiling, plus a MkdirAll of
<repo>/.entire/tmp, during what reads as a read-only probe. agent.List() is
alphabetical, so opencode was probed before pi and vogon.

This is the same reason PrepareTranscript is gated behind an os.Stat (see the
comment there about Cursor's 3s poll); agent-side materialization is strictly
more expensive than a flush.

Thread an explicit transcriptLookup through resolveAndValidateTranscript:
lookupAllowFetch for the agent the user named, lookupLocalOnly while probing the
others. Because detection no longer exports on the user's behalf, the
transcript-not-found error now names the agents that could have, so someone who
omitted or mistyped --agent gets the one-flag fix instead of "is the session ID
correct?".

TestAttach_TranscriptNotFound: 1.05s -> 0.13s.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text: Two decisions worth confirming before I write the plan. (Items 1 and 2 I'll just decide — see below.)

questions.question: For the hint (item 3): nothing in the repo knows an agent's session-ID shape today (validation.ValidateSessionID is generic path-safety only), so a precise gate would mean inventing a per-agent capability just for a hint. How should the hint be made non-misleading?

options.label: Conditional \nHint: line (Recommended)
options.description: Pure wording/formatting change. Reuses the existing `\nHint: ...` convention (checkpoint_resume.go:147,155, explain.go:306) and phrases the suggestion conditionally, so it is never wrong — a typo'd ID just sees an offer it can ignore. No new machinery, no behavior change.
options.preview:
transcript not found for agent "claude-code" with session
abc123; is the session ID correct? (also tried auto-detecting
other agents: transcript not found for any registered agent)
Hint: if this session belongs to OpenCode, retry with
--agent opencode — OpenCode can export transcripts on demand.

options.label: Gate on session-ID shape
options.description: Only emit the hint when the ID could plausibly belong to a fetcher agent (e.g. OpenCode's `ses_` prefix). Precise, but requires a new per-agent ID-shape notion that does not exist today — a new interface or a hardcoded prefix in attach.go — to serve one hint string.

options.label: Leave it unconditional
options.description: Drop item 3. The hint stays exactly as shipped: every transcript-not-found under a non-fetcher agent ends with `retry with --agent opencode`. Useful when the agent was wrong, noise when the ID was mistyped.

questions.question: For context cancellation (item 4): the canceled fetch currently escapes the transcriptFetchError suppression, so detectAgentByTranscript still runs its full stat loop on a dead context and its failure gets appended. How wide should the fix be?

options.label: Guard auto-detection on ctx too (Recommended)
options.description: Wrap the canceled fetch error in transcriptFetchError (so the suppression branch fires as its comment claims) AND return early from resolveAgentAndTranscript when ctx is already done. Covers Ctrl-C for every agent, not just fetchers — detection is pure stat calls today and never notices cancellation.

options.label: Wrap the canceled error only
options.description: Minimal, targeted: wrap the canceled fetch error in transcriptFetchError so the existing suppression branch catches it. Ctrl-C under a fetcher agent is clean; Ctrl-C under a non-fetcher agent still runs the pointless detection loop.

# Follow-ups to the OpenCode on-demand transcript fetch (PR #1877)

## Context

PR #1877 (now merged) added the `TranscriptFetcher` capability so `entire attach`
can materialize an OpenCode transcript for sessions Entire never tracked, and
introduced staged exports so a failed `opencode export` can no longer destroy the
cached transcript. Four loose ends came out of review. None is a correctness bug;
all four are polish on the surfaces a user or a future agent-integrator actually
touches.

1. `TranscriptFetcher` is the only optional agent capability with no entry in the
   agent-integration docs — the repo documents every other one.
2. The rename-failure message says "failed to install export file" twice.
3. The retry hint tells the user *what* to do but makes them assemble the command.
4. A canceled fetch escapes the `transcriptFetchError` suppression, so the
   comment claiming it is suppressed is not true.

## 1. Document `TranscriptFetcher`

`docs/architecture/agent-guide.md`

- Add a row to the **Optional Interfaces** table (~line 50), immediately after
  `TranscriptPreparer` so the pair reads together:

  | `TranscriptFetcher` | `FetchTranscript` | Agent can export a transcript on demand, including for sessions Entire never tracked (no hook-cached file exists) |

- Add a `### TranscriptFetcher` section immediately after the existing
  `### TranscriptPreparer` section (~line 484), in the same
  What-it-enables / Without-it / Implement-when / Method shape. The load-bearing
  point is the contrast with `TranscriptPreparer`: **Preparer refreshes a file
  that already exists; Fetcher conjures one that never did.** Also state:
  - `FetchTranscript(ctx, sessionID) (string, error)` writes to the agent's cache
    location and returns that path.
  - Errors are shown to users after other transcript sources fail, so they must
    be concise and safe to display (see `classifyOpenCodeExportError` in
    `cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/cli_commands.go`).
  - It is a builtin-only capability — no `DeclaredCaps` gate, resolved by
    `agent.AsTranscriptFetcher` type assertion alone, same as
    `TranscriptSanitizer`.
  - It is called only for the agent the user named, never during auto-detection
    (`transcriptLookup` in `cmd/entire/cli/attach.go`).

`docs/architecture/agent-integration-checklist.md`

- Line 44: add `[TranscriptFetcher](agent-guide.md#transcriptfetcher)` to the
  "See Guide:" list.
- Add one checklist bullet under **Transcript Capture**, after the
  "Use agent's canonical export" bullet:
  - [ ] **On-demand export**: if the agent can produce a transcript for a session
    Entire never hooked, implement `TranscriptFetcher` so `entire attach` works
    for externally-spawned sessions

## 2. Collapse the doubled error prefix

`renameOverExisting` owns the "failed to install export file" phrasing on **both**
branches (fixing the current asymmetry where only the early return carries it);
`fetchAndCacheExport` contributes only the recovery clause.

`cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/stage_export.go`

- Line 58 — unchanged.
- Line 62 — gain the prefix:
  ```go
  return fmt.Errorf("failed to install export file: %w (another process may be reading %s)",
      err, filepath.Base(dest))
  ```

`cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/lifecycle.go:274` — drop the prefix, keep the path:

```go
return "", fmt.Errorf("%w (export saved at %s)", err, staged)
```

Resulting message:
`failed to install export file: rename a b: permission denied (export saved at /repo/.entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-1)`

Keep the `%w` wraps — `wrapcheck` is enabled and `stage_export.go` is not in the
`.golangci.yaml` exclusions, so a bare `return err` at line 58 is not available.

## 3. Make the hint a copy-pasteable command

`cmd/entire/cli/attach.go` — `unprobedFetcherHint` (line 799) takes the session ID
and emits a full command on its own line, following the in-error `\nHint:`
convention already used by `checkpoint_resume.go:147` and `explain.go:306`:

```go
func unprobedFetcherHint(tried types.AgentName, sessionID string) string {
    // ...existing loop over agent.List() collecting fetcher names, unchanged...
    if len(names) == 0 {
        return ""
    }
    // A pathological session ID must not be echoed into a command we invite the
    // user to paste into a shell. Reuse the existing path-safe validator: every
    // real agent session ID (UUIDs, ses_*, date-prefixed UUIDs) passes it.
    if validation.ValidateAgentSessionID(sessionID) != nil {
        return fmt.Sprintf("\nHint: %s can export transcripts on demand — retry with --agent %s",
            strings.Join(names, " and "), names[0])
    }
    return fmt.Sprintf("\nHint: %s can export transcripts on demand:\n  entire attach %s --agent %s",
        strings.Join(names, " and "), sessionID, names[0])
}
```

Call site (line 783) passes `sessionID` and drops the `%s`-suffix concatenation
into the same position it occupies today. `validation` is already imported
(attach.go:27). The command stays bare — no `--force` / `--review` reproduction,
so the hint never has to track flags attach gains later.

## 4. Wrap the canceled fetch error

`cmd/entire/cli/attach.go` — in `resolveAndValidateTranscript`, the
`context.Canceled` early return currently bypasses the suppression branch at line
772, so `detectAgentByTranscript` still runs and its failure is appended:

```go
if errors.Is(fetchErr, context.Canceled) {
    return "", &transcriptFetchError{cause: fmt.Errorf("fetch transcript: %w", fetchErr)}
}
```

The early return itself stays — skipping the project-dir search on cancellation is
correct. Scope is deliberately just this: for a non-fetcher agent there is no
fetch to cancel, and guarding auto-detection on `ctx` would only skip a loop of
stat calls.

## Tests

`cmd/entire/cli/attach_test.go`
- `TestUnprobedFetcherHint` — new signature; assert the full
  `entire attach <id> --agent opencode` line for a path-safe ID, and that a
  non-path-safe ID (e.g. `"weird id"`) falls back to the prose form without
  echoing the ID into a command.
- `TestAttach_TranscriptNotFound` — tighten the `--agent opencode` substring
  assertion to the full command line.

## Context

PR #1877 (now merged) added the `TranscriptFetcher` capability so `entire attach`
can materialize an OpenCode transcript for sessions Entire never tracked, and
introduced staged exports so a failed `opencode export` can no longer destroy the
cached transcript. Four loose ends came out of review. None is a correctness bug;
all four are polish on the surfaces a user or a future agent-integrator actually
touches.

1. `TranscriptFetcher` is the only optional agent capability with no entry in the
   agent-integration docs — the repo documents every other one.
2. The rename-failure message says "failed to install export file" twice.
3. The retry hint tells the user *what* to do but makes them assemble the command.
4. A canceled fetch escapes the `transcriptFetchError` suppression, so the
   comment claiming it is suppressed is not true.

## 1. Document `TranscriptFetcher`

`docs/architecture/agent-guide.md`

- Add a row to the **Optional Interfaces** table (~line 50), immediately after
  `TranscriptPreparer` so the pair reads together:

  | `TranscriptFetcher` | `FetchTranscript` | Agent can export a transcript on demand, including for sessions Entire never tracked (no hook-cached file exists) |

- Add a `### TranscriptFetcher` section immediately after the existing
  `### TranscriptPreparer` section (~line 484), in the same
  What-it-enables / Without-it / Implement-when / Method shape. The load-bearing
  point is the contrast with `TranscriptPreparer`: **Preparer refreshes a file
  that already exists; Fetcher conjures one that never did.** Also state:
  - `FetchTranscript(ctx, sessionID) (string, error)` writes to the agent's cache
    location and returns that path.
  - Errors are shown to users after other transcript sources fail, so they must
    be concise and safe to display (see `classifyOpenCodeExportError` in
    `cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/cli_commands.go`).
  - It is a builtin-only capability — no `DeclaredCaps` gate, resolved by
    `agent.AsTranscriptFetcher` type assertion alone, same as
    `TranscriptSanitizer`.
  - It is called only for the agent the user named, never during auto-detection
    (`transcriptLookup` in `cmd/entire/cli/attach.go`).

`docs/architecture/agent-integration-checklist.md`

- Line 44: add `[TranscriptFetcher](agent-guide.md#transcriptfetcher)` to the
  "See Guide:" list.

    for externally-spawned sessions

branches (fixing the current asymmetry where only the early return carries it);

```go
return "", fmt.Errorf("%w (export saved at %s)", err, staged)
```

`.golangci.yaml` exclusions, so a bare `return err` at line 58 is not available.

and emits a full command on its own line, following the in-error `\nHint:`

```go
func unprobedFetcherHint(tried types.AgentName, sessionID string) string {
```

`docs/architecture/agent-guide.md`

  What-it-enables / Without-it / Implement-when / Method shape. The load-bearing

  that already exists; Fetcher conjures one that never did.** Also state:
  - `FetchTranscript(ctx, sessionID) (string, error)` writes to the agent's cache

```go
func unprobedFetcherHint(tried types.AgentName, sessionID string) string {
    // ...existing loop over agent.List() collecting fetcher names, unchanged...
    if len(names) == 0 {
        return ""
    }
    // A pathological session ID must not be echoed into a command we invite the
    // user to paste into a shell. Reuse the existing path-safe validator: every
    // real agent session ID (UUIDs, ses_*, date-prefixed UUIDs) passes it.
    if validation.ValidateAgentSessionID(sessionID) != nil {

            strings.Join(names, " and "), names[0])
    }
    return fmt.Sprintf("\nHint: %s can export transcripts on demand:\n  entire attach %s --agent %s",
        strings.Join(names, " and "), sessionID, names[0])
```

**What it enables:** Token usage metrics in checkpoint metadata"""
section = """### `TranscriptFetcher`

**What it enables:** `entire attach` on a session Entire never tracked — one spawned by an external session host rather than a hooked terminal, where no hook ever cached a transcript.

**Without it:** Attach can only work from a transcript already on disk, so an untracked session fails with "transcript not found".

**Implement when:** Your agent can produce a full transcript for an arbitrary session ID on request (e.g. OpenCode's `opencode export <id>`).

**Not the same as `TranscriptPreparer`:** Preparer refreshes a file that already exists; Fetcher conjures one that never did. An agent that writes asynchronously wants Preparer; an agent with an export command wants Fetcher. Implementing both is fine.

**Method:**
- `FetchTranscript(sessionID) (path, error)` - Write the transcript to the agent's cache location and return that path.

**Contract:**
- **Errors are user-facing.** They surface after every other transcript source has failed, so return concise, safe-to-display messages rather than raw subprocess output. See `classifyOpenCodeExportError` in `opencode/cli_commands.go`, which maps a missing binary / unknown session / timeout to one sentence each and redacts anything it echoes from stderr.
- **Never write in place.** Callers may already hold the only local copy of the session at the destination path; export to a staging file, validate it, then rename. See `stageExportPath` / `renameOverExisting` in `opencode/stage_export.go`.
- **Builtin-only capability.** There is no `DeclaredCaps` gate — `agent.AsTranscriptFetcher` resolves by type assertion alone, like `TranscriptSanitizer`.
- **Called only for the agent the user named.** Attach threads a `transcriptLookup` through transcript resolution (`cmd/entire/cli/attach.go`) so auto-detection, which probes every registered agent, never spawns your export subprocess on the user's behalf.

"""

+| `TranscriptFetcher` | `FetchTranscript` | Agent can export a transcript on demand, including for sessions Entire never tracked (no hook-cached file exists) |
 | `TokenCalculator` | `CalculateTokenUsage` | Agent's transcript contains token usage data |
 | `SubagentAwareExtractor` | `ExtractAllModifiedFiles`, `CalculateTotalTokenUsage` | Agent spawns subagents (like Claude Code's Task tool) |
 | `SubagentSessionResolver` | `ResolveSubagentSession` | Agent runs subagents as **detached sessions of their own** rather than as a blocking tool call (Factory AI Droid's Workers) |
@@ -483,6 +484,25 @@ The framework dispatcher (`DispatchLifecycleEvent` in `lifecycle.go`) handles ea
 **Method:**
 - `PrepareTranscript(sessionRef) error` - Wait until the transcript is fully written. Called before `ReadTranscript`.
 
+### `TranscriptFetcher`
+
+**What it enables:** `entire attach` on a session Entire never tracked — one spawned by an external session host rather than a hooked terminal, where no hook ever cached a transcript.
+
+**Without it:** Attach can only work from a transcript already on disk, so an untracked session fails with "transcript not found".
+
+**Implement when:** Your agent can produce a full transcript for an arbitrary session ID on request (e.g. OpenCode's `opencode export <id>`).
+
+**Not the same as `TranscriptPreparer`:** Preparer refreshes a file that already exists; Fetcher conjures one that never did. An agent that writes asynchronously wants Preparer; an agent with an export command wants Fetcher. Implementing both is fine.
+
+**Method:**
+- `FetchTranscript(sessionID) (path, error)` - Write the transcript to the agent's cache location and return that path.
+
+**Contract:**
+- **Errors are user-facing.** They surface after every other transcript source has failed, so return concise, safe-to-display messages rather than raw subprocess output. See `classifyOpenCodeExportError` in `opencode/cli_commands.go`, which maps a missing binary / unknown session / timeout to one sentence each and redacts anything it echoes from stderr.
+- **Never write in place.** Callers may already hold the only local copy of the session at the destination path; export to a staging file, validate it, then rename. See `stageExportPath` / `renameOverExisting` in `opencode/stage_export.go`.
+- **Builtin-only capability.** There is no `DeclaredCaps` gate — `agent.AsTranscriptFetcher` resolves by type assertion alone, like `TranscriptSanitizer`.
+- **Called only for the agent the user named.** Attach threads a `transcriptLookup` through transcript resolution (`cmd/entire/cli/attach.go`) so auto-detection, which probes every registered agent, never spawns your export subprocess on the user's behalf.
+
 ### `TokenCalculator`
 
 **What it enables:** Token usage metrics in checkpoint metadata (input, output, cache tokens, API call count).

 - [ ] **Full transcript on every turn**: At turn-end, capture the complete session transcript, not just events since the last checkpoint
 - [ ] **Resumed session handling**: When a user resumes an existing session, the transcript must include all historical messages, not just new ones since the plugin/hook loaded
 - [ ] **Use agent's canonical export**: Prefer the agent's native export command (e.g., reading Claude's JSONL file, Gemini's JSON, Cursor's JSONL, Factory AI Droid's JSONL, Copilot CLI's JSONL, OpenCode's `opencode export` JSON, Pi's JSONL session file) over manually reconstructing from events
+- [ ] **On-demand export**: If the agent can produce a transcript for a session Entire never hooked (e.g. one spawned by an external session host), implement `TranscriptFetcher` so `entire attach` works for it instead of failing with "transcript not found"

 - [ ] **Graceful degradation**: If the canonical source is unavailable (e.g., agent shutting down), fall back to best-effort capture with clear documentation of limitations

Default the plan and the implementation to KISS + DRY + TDD. Concrete application:

- **KISS**: simplest working thing. Cut optional structs/flags/scaffolding unless they earn their keep in this iteration. Prefer one string field over a new struct. Do not add speculative "future-proof" layers.
- **DRY**: factor shared helpers into a single place before adding the second call site — not after. When a plan has repeated "do X in file A, also do X in file B", collapse to one helper.
- **TDD**: write the failing test first, then the minimal code to pass, then refactor. Plans should list the test as the first work item for each behavior, not an afterthought at the end.

**Why**: on 2026-04-22 a plan for Cursor export/import was rejected with "kiss, dry and tdd" — it over-structured the archive schema (WorkspaceMapping struct where a string sufficed), scattered similar discovery logic, and bundled tests at the end instead of driving each phase.

**How to apply**: when writing a plan file in plan mode, order each phase as `failing test → minimal code → refactor`, call out the shared helper before listing its call sites, and strip any field/flag/doc that is not required to satisfy a test in this iteration.

All four items done, uncommitted in the working tree.

**1. Docs** — `TranscriptFetcher` now has a row in `agent-guide.md`'s Optional Interfaces table plus a `### TranscriptFetcher` section (line 487) covering the `TranscriptPreparer` contrast, the user-facing-errors rule, the never-write-in-place rule, the builtin-only resolution, and the named-agent-only call site. `agent-integration-checklist.md` gained the guide link and an **On-demand export** bullet.

**2. Error prefix** — `renameOverExisting` owns `failed to install export file:` on both branches; `fetchAndCacheExport` contributes only `(export saved at …)`. I confirmed the new test discriminates: reverting just the caller line makes `TestFetchAndCacheExport_FailedInstallKeepsStagedExport` fail on "named once, not once per wrapping layer".

**3. Hint** — now a pasteable command. Verified against a real binary in a scratch repo:

```
transcript not found for agent "claude-code" with session 00000000-...-000000000000; is the session ID correct? (also tried auto-detecting other agents: transcript not found for any registered agent)
Hint: opencode can export transcripts on demand:
  entire session attach 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --agent opencode
```

**4. Cancellation** — the canceled fetch is wrapped in `transcriptFetchError`, scope kept to exactly that.

## Two things worth your attention

**`main` did not compile.** The merge commit `fe80c26d2` dropped `clean.go`'s `logging` import — it's present on the branch, absent after the merge, and `logging.Debug` at `clean.go:485` needs it. A semantic merge conflict, so it wasn't a textual conflict anyone would have seen. I restored the import; that's why `clean.go` appears in the diff.

**`entire attach` is a deprecated form.** `TestNoDeprecatedCommandFormsInUserFacingStrings` caught my first draft of the hint — the canonical spelling is `entire session attach`, otherwise the CLI hands out advice that triggers its own deprecation warning. Fixed in the hint, the tests, and the two doc mentions. Good guard; it found a real bug in my work.

## Tests added

- `TestUnprobedFetcherHint` — asserts the full command line; new `_UnsafeSessionIDIsNotSpelledIntoACommand` covers the path-safe gate (`oops; rm -rf ~` gets prose, and the ID is not echoed at all).
- `TestResolveAndValidateTranscript_CanceledFetchIsSuppressible` — `errors.As` finds `*transcriptFetchError` and the chain retains `context.Canceled`.
- `TestRenameOverExisting_NamesTheFailureOnce` and `TestFetchAndCacheExport_FailedInstallKeepsStagedExport` — the rename-failure path, previously uncovered; the second also pins that the validated staged export is *kept*, not deleted. Both force the failure with a directory at `dest`, so they work on every platform without stubbing `os.Rename`.

Verification: `mise run fmt`, `golangci-lint 2.11.3 run ./...` → 0 issues (run after fmt), full unit suite → no failures, `mise run test:integration` → all PASS, `GOOS=windows go build ./...` → OK. I have not committed — say the word and I'll stage it, though the `clean.go` import fix arguably belongs in its own commit since it's a merge repair rather than review follow-up.

content.text:
Item 2 done. On item 1, the evidence says it isn't duplication — details below.

## Item 2 — `lifecycle` now owns the wording

Net effect is a **one-line change**, and it's in `stage_export.go` only. `lifecycle.go:274` is back to exactly what was merged, so the shipped message is unchanged:

```
failed to install export file (export saved at .entire/tmp/.export-ses_install_fails-316818213): rename .entire/tmp/.export-ses_install_fails-316818213 .entire/tmp/ses_install_fails.json: file exists
```

The bare `return err` does trip wrapcheck (`error returned from external package is unwrapped: sig: func os.Rename`), so it carries `//nolint:wrapcheck` with the required explanation plus a comment saying why it's deliberately raw.

Tests followed the ownership flip: `TestRenameOverExisting_NamesTheFailureOnce` became `..._LeavesUserFacingWordingToTheCaller` — it now asserts the function does *not* add that sentence and that `os.Rename`'s `*os.LinkError` passes through. The end-to-end `TestFetchAndCacheExport_FailedInstallKeepsStagedExport` still pins "exactly once"; I re-checked that it discriminates by putting the prefix back into `stage_export.go` — both tests fail.

Verification: lint 0 issues repo-wide, `GOOS=windows go build ./...` OK, full unit suite clean.

## Item 1 — different check, not a duplicate

You're right that there's an upstream fail-fast: `validateAttachPreconditions` calls `validation.ValidateSessionID` at `attach.go:740`, before the hint is ever built. But that validator answers a different question — *is this safe in a file path* — and it permits spaces, `;`, `$`, `&`. It rejects only `/ \ : * ? [`, leading dashes, `.`/`..`, and absolute paths. (`validators_test.go` treats `session-2026.01.25_test@123` as valid input.)

So an unsafe ID reaches the hint. Built binary, scratch repo, argv passed as a list so no shell was involved:

```
$ entire session attach 'oops; rm -rf ~'
transcript not found for agent "claude-code" with session oops; rm -rf ~; is the session ID correct? (...)
Hint: opencode can export transcripts on demand — retry with --agent opencode        ← prose fallback

$ entire session attach ok-uuid-1234
Hint: opencode can export transcripts on demand:
  entire session attach ok-uuid-1234 --agent opencode                                 ← command form
```

Without the second check, the first case prints `entire session attach oops; rm -rf ~ --agent opencode` as something we're inviting the user to paste into a shell.

Two ways to remove the duplication for real, if the second call still bothers you:

1. **Tighten upstream** — have `validateAttachPreconditions` use `ValidateAgentSessionID` (`^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`) so one check covers both concerns. Cheaper and genuinely DRY, but it narrows what `attach` accepts, and I can't yet prove no agent uses `.` or `@` in a session ID — Pi accepts partial UUIDs, and the validator's own comment says formats vary per agent. Would need a pass over the agents first.
2. **Drop the gate** — accept that a pathological ID gets echoed into a suggested command. Low likelihood, since the ID is something the user typed themselves.

Say which and I'll do it; option 1 is the one that actually satisfies the DRY complaint, so I'd start by checking whether any agent's IDs fall outside the strict pattern.

## Item 2 — my answer is no, and here's the concrete reason

I looked for text worth adding and couldn't find any that isn't already on the wire. The message today:

```
failed to install export file (export saved at .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213): rename .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213 .entire/tmp/ses_x.json: file exists
```

`*os.LinkError` already carries the operation, **both** paths, and the cause. Going through the candidates:

| Candidate text | Already said by |
| --- | --- |
| what we were doing (`rename`) | `LinkError` |
| source / destination paths | `LinkError` (staged path twice, counting lifecycle's) |
| the cause (`file exists`) | `LinkError` |
| why it matters ("installing an export") | `lifecycle.go` |
| what to do ("export saved at …") | `lifecycle.go` |

The only fact not on the wire is *"we did not retry"* — and that one is actively misleading to add, because `isRenameContention` is hardcoded `false` on POSIX, so **every** non-Windows failure takes this branch. Telling a Mac user their rename "was not retried" implies a retry existed to skip.

So any wrap here would be a third mention of something already present — which is the exact problem you just had me fix. The `//nolint:wrapcheck` is doing real work: it documents at the site that raw is deliberate, which a redundant wrap would hide.

If the inline nolint itself is what you'd rather avoid, the repo's precedent is a `.golangci.yaml` path exclusion — `configloader.go` has one for the same "must return the raw error" reason. I'd still keep the inline version: it's one line instead of a config entry, and it won't silence a future genuine wrapcheck hit elsewhere in `stage_export.go`.

Still uncommitted. The `clean.go` import restore is a merge repair rather than review follow-up, so I'd put it in its own commit ahead of the rest — say the word and I'll split and stage it that way.

# Ship Changes

Commit current changes, push to remote, and update the PR.

## Step 1: Analyze changes

1. Run `git diff --stat` and `git diff` to understand what changed
2. Run `git status` to see untracked files
3. Run `git log --oneline -3` to match the repo's commit message style

## Step 2: Commit

1. Stage only the relevant changed/untracked files by name (never `git add -A` or `git add .`)
2. Write a concise commit message that focuses on the "why" not the "what"
   - If `` is provided, use it as the commit message
   - Otherwise, draft one from the diff
3. Commit. If hooks fail, diagnose and fix — do NOT use `--no-verify`

## Step 3: Push

1. Check if the branch tracks a remote: `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u}`
2. If not tracking, push with `-u origin <branch>`
3. If tracking, just `git push`
4. If push is rejected (remote has new commits), pull with rebase first then push

## Step 4: Update PR

1. Find the open PR for the current branch: `gh pr view --json number,body,title`
2. If no PR exists, skip this step and inform the user
3. Compare the current PR body against the new changes:
   - If the changes are within the existing PR scope, update the description to reflect the current state
   - If the changes are additive or a follow-up, add a PR comment summarizing what was just pushed instead
4. When updating the PR body, preserve the overall structure but refresh the summary bullets and test plan
5. When adding a comment, keep it concise — bullet points of what changed and why
6. **Before making any PR update (description edit or comment), show the user the exact text you plan to post and ask for their approval. Do NOT post until they confirm.**

## Rules

- Never commit files that look like secrets (.env, credentials, tokens)
- Never force push

fix(attach): hand the user the retry command, not the flag to add

unprobedFetcherHint told the user which --agent flag to add and left them to

the `\nHint:` convention in checkpoint_resume.go / explain.go, and spells the

`opencode export` got the secondary auto-detection failure appended to it. Wrap
it, which is all the comment at the suppression branch ever claimed.

renameOverExisting and its caller both said "failed to install export file", so
a rename that could not land reported it twice in one message. fetchAndCacheExport
keeps the wording — it is the one that also knows where the validated export was
kept — and the rename passes os.Rename's error through raw, which already carries
the operation, both paths, and the cause.

Also documents TranscriptFetcher, the one optional agent capability with no entry
in the integration docs. The load-bearing distinction: TranscriptPreparer
refreshes a file that already exists, TranscriptFetcher conjures one that never
did.

Tests: the rename-failure path was uncovered. Both new cases force it with a
directory at the destination, so they need no os.Rename stub and behave the same
on every platform.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

import subprocess

Four loose ends from reviewing #1877 (OpenCode on-demand transcript fetch). No correctness bugs — all four are on surfaces a user or a future agent-integrator actually touches.

## What changed

**The retry hint is now a command, not a flag to assemble.** `unprobedFetcherHint` told the user which `--agent` to add; it now prints the whole line, following the `\\nHint:` convention in `checkpoint_resume.go` / `explain.go`:

```
transcript not found for agent "claude-code" with session 00000000-...-000000000000; is the session ID correct? (also tried auto-detecting other agents: transcript not found for any registered agent)
Hint: opencode can export transcripts on demand:
  entire session attach 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --agent opencode
```

It spells the canonical `entire session attach`, not the deprecated top-level form — `TestNoDeprecatedCommandFormsInUserFacingStrings` caught the first draft, since a hint that trips the CLI's own deprecation warning is advice the CLI gave itself.

**A canceled fetch no longer drags auto-detection noise along.** Ctrl-C during `opencode export` escaped the `transcriptFetchError` suppression, so the secondary "also tried auto-detecting other agents" failure got appended to a cancellation. Wrapping it is all the comment at the suppression branch ever claimed. Scope stops there: for a non-fetcher agent there is no fetch to cancel, and guarding auto-detection on `ctx` would only skip a loop of stat calls.

**"failed to install export file" was printed twice in one message.** `renameOverExisting` and `fetchAndCacheExport` both supplied it. The caller keeps the wording — it is also the one that knows where the validated export was kept — and the rename returns `os.Rename`'s error raw, which already carries the operation, both paths, and the cause:

```
failed to install export file (export saved at .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213): rename .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213 .entire/tmp/ses_x.json: file exists
```

The bare return needs `//nolint:wrapcheck` (wrapcheck flags unwrapped stdlib errors and `stage_export.go` is not excluded); the comment says why raw is deliberate.

**`TranscriptFetcher` is documented.** It was the only optional agent capability with no entry in `agent-guide.md` or the integration checklist. The load-bearing distinction: `TranscriptPreparer` refreshes a file that already exists, `TranscriptFetcher` conjures one that never did. The section also records the contract that is easy to get wrong — errors are user-facing, never write in place, builtin-only capability, called only for the agent the user named.

## Test plan

The rename-failure path was uncovered. Both new cases force it with a directory at the destination, so they need no `os.Rename` stub and behave identically on every platform.

- `TestRenameOverExisting_LeavesUserFacingWordingToTheCaller` — pins the ownership split: the function must not add the caller's sentence, and `*os.LinkError` passes through.
- `TestFetchAndCacheExport_FailedInstallKeepsStagedExport` — end-to-end: prefix appears exactly once, and the validated export is *kept*, not deleted. Verified this discriminates by putting the prefix back into `stage_export.go` — both tests fail.

- `TestUnprobedFetcherHint` / `TestAttach_TranscriptNotFound` — assert the full command line.

content.text: The trail opened a **draft** PR with a placeholder body. Per the ship skill I won't post without your OK — here's the exact body I'd set, preserving the trail-link markers at the top:

input.command:
cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gtrrz-victor-wks-cli-release-nightly/ec8dd25d-fa92-4d10-9f5f-ea16b98a9508/scratchpad/pr-body.md <<'EOF'
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1130
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Why

Four loose ends from reviewing #1877 (OpenCode on-demand transcript fetch). No correctness bugs — all four sit on surfaces a user or a future agent-integrator actually touches.

## What changed

**The retry hint is a command now, not a flag to assemble.** `unprobedFetcherHint` named the `--agent` to add and left the rest to the reader. It prints the whole line, following the `\nHint:` convention in `checkpoint_resume.go` / `explain.go`:

```
transcript not found for agent "claude-code" with session 00000000-...-000000000000; is the session ID correct? (also tried auto-detecting other agents: transcript not found for any registered agent)
Hint: opencode can export transcripts on demand:
  entire session attach 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --agent opencode
```

It spells the canonical `entire session attach`, not the deprecated top-level form. `TestNoDeprecatedCommandFormsInUserFacingStrings` caught the first draft — a hint that trips the CLI's own deprecation warning is advice the CLI gave itself.

**A canceled fetch no longer drags auto-detection noise along.** Ctrl-C during `opencode export` escaped the `transcriptFetchError` suppression, so the secondary "also tried auto-detecting other agents" failure got appended to a cancellation. Wrapping it is all the comment at the suppression branch ever claimed. Scope stops there: a non-fetcher agent has no fetch to cancel, and guarding auto-detection on `ctx` would only skip a loop of stat calls.

**"failed to install export file" was printed twice in one message.** `renameOverExisting` and `fetchAndCacheExport` both supplied it. The caller keeps the wording — it is also the one that knows where the validated export was kept — and the rename returns `os.Rename`'s error raw, which already carries the operation, both paths, and the cause:

```
failed to install export file (export saved at .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213): rename .entire/tmp/.export-ses_x-316818213 .entire/tmp/ses_x.json: file exists
```

The bare return needs `//nolint:wrapcheck` — wrapcheck flags unwrapped stdlib errors and `stage_export.go` is not excluded — and the comment says why raw is deliberate.

**`TranscriptFetcher` is documented.** It was the only optional agent capability absent from `agent-guide.md` and the integration checklist. The load-bearing distinction: `TranscriptPreparer` refreshes a file that already exists, `TranscriptFetcher` conjures one that never did. The section also records the contract that is easy to get wrong — errors are user-facing, never write in place, builtin-only capability, called only for the agent the user named.

## Test plan

The rename-failure path was uncovered. Both new cases force it with a directory at the destination, so they need no `os.Rename` stub and behave identically on every platform.

- `TestRenameOverExisting_LeavesUserFacingWordingToTheCaller` — pins the ownership split: the function must not add the caller's sentence, and `*os.LinkError` passes through.
- `TestFetchAndCacheExport_FailedInstallKeepsStagedExport` — end-to-end: the prefix appears exactly once, and the validated export is *kept*, not deleted. I checked this discriminates by putting the prefix back into `stage_export.go` — both tests fail.
- `TestResolveAndValidateTranscript_CanceledFetchIsSuppressible` — `errors.As` finds `*transcriptFetchError` and the chain retains `context.Canceled`.
- `TestUnprobedFetcherHint` / `TestAttach_TranscriptNotFound` — assert the full command line.

Verified: `mise run fmt`, `golangci-lint 2.11.3 run ./...` → 0 issues (run after fmt), full unit suite, `mise run test:integration` → all PASS, `GOOS=windows go build ./...`, plus a manual run of the built binary in a scratch repo to check the rendered hint.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
